title: How to cut a pizza into 11 slices with 4 cuts
description:
Four straight cuts through the middle give 8 slices; four cuts placed so that every new cut crosses all the earlier ones inside the crust, never at a shared point, give 11. A new cut adds one piece, plus one more for every cut it crosses, so n cuts give at most 1 + (1 + 2 + ... + n) pieces: 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, and 56 with 10 cuts (against 20 through the middle). This is the lazy caterer's sequence.

Numbers checked in code: the formula for 1 to 10 cuts, and 100,000 random sets of cuts that never beat it. Source: Wikipedia, Lazy caterer's sequence.

social_caption: Four straight cuts through the middle give 8 slices of pizza. Four smarter cuts give 11, and the rule behind it is one line.
facts_checked: Through the middle: n cuts = 2n slices (4 -> 8, 10 -> 20); best placement: (n^2 + n + 2)/2 = 2, 4, 7, 11, 16 for 1-5 cuts, 56 for 10; cut 3 through the middle gives 6, off-centre 7; cut 4 adds 4; 100,000 random sets of 5 chords never beat the formula and reach it (verify.py)

Lazy caterer's sequence: maximum pieces with n straight cuts = (n^2 + n + 2)/2; the nth cut crosses the n - 1 earlier cuts, is split into n segments, each splitting one piece in two, adding n pieces (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazy_caterer%27s_sequence)

beats.say: Your pizza has to feed 11 people. No stacking, no folding. Four straight cuts. Not one more.
Cut one: two pieces. Cut two, straight across it: four.
Cut three is where everyone goes wrong. Through the middle, you get six. Miss the middle, so it crosses both cuts in different spots: seven.
That's the rule. A new cut adds one piece, plus one for every cut it crosses.
So cut four has to cross all three. Is there even room?
Tilt it, so it hits all three inside the crust. That's three crossings, four new pieces. 11.
Each cut adds one more than the last. 10 cuts give 56 slices, not 20. Nobody said they'd be equal.
